title: State, Identity, and the Cost of Uncertainty

sections.title: API Contracts and Durable Operation Records
Recording Intent Before the Remote Call

html:
Picture an evening of online shopping. You find a jacket you like in your favorite shopping app, add it to your cart, enter your card details, and press Pay. The confirmation screen shows a spinner, the spinner turns and turns, and finally the app shows an error. Did the money leave your account? The order history shows nothing new, so pressing Pay again feels harmless. Somewhere else, though, the payment provider may already have approved the first attempt, and the only thing lost was the reply. The same moment comes up when you book a hotel room or renew a subscription.

That is what happened to a Baodium customer during a promotion. The customer pressed Pay, saw no confirmation, and pressed it again. Checkout recorded one order. The provider recorded two authorizations, and the customer saw two pending charges on their card.

When the payments engineers traced the two requests, the code had done what it was written to do. The first authorization had succeeded at the provider, but the response never reached Checkout Service. Checkout treated the timeout as a failed payment, so when the customer tried again, it started a brand new authorization. The actual gap was in the design. A timeout shows only that the caller stopped waiting, not what happened at the other end, and checkout had no record that would let it recognize the second click as the same purchase.

Idempotent Operations and Retry Safety

An operation is idempotent if performing it twice has the same effect as performing it once. A light switch labeled “on” is idempotent. Press it ten times and the light is on. A switch that toggles is different, because pressing it twice returns the light to its original state.

Many operations are naturally idempotent. “Set the shipping address to 12 Market Street” can be repeated safely. “Add $100 to the balance” or “authorize a $100 payment” cannot, because each repetition adds another effect. To make these operations safe to retry, we can assign an identifier to each intended action. The receiving service records that identifier and checks it before applying another effect. A paper cheque works this way. Each one carries a number, and a bank that is handed the same cheque twice will not pay it twice, because it recognizes the number. The implementation must define which operation is being repeated and which state change is permitted.

Timeouts and Uncertain Remote Outcomes

A card authorization reserves funds, while a later capture collects them. Two authorizations can reserve funds twice even when checkout ultimately records a single order. That distinction mattered to the customer whose first attempt had succeeded without a confirmation.

In the Baodium incident, the provider had completed the first authorization. Checkout recorded the attempt as failed because no response arrived, and when the customer clicked Pay again, it submitted a new, independent authorization. At no point did checkout’s database contain a record of what the provider had done.

After the incident, the team changed the handler. When it could not confirm the result, it now recorded the outcome as unresolved instead of failed. The page told the customer that the payment was being verified, and clicking Pay again retrieved the existing payment operation instead of starting a new one.

The team also disabled the Pay button after the first click. That reduced accidental double clicks, but a customer could still refresh the page or open a second tab. A client library that retries automatically, a second browser tab, or a mobile app that resends a request after a network change can all submit the payment again, so the server has to recognize repeated submissions itself. For that, checkout needs a durable record of the authorization it intends to perform, and the record must exist before the provider call, because the handler can stop at any moment after it sends the request.

API Contracts and Durable Operation Records

We can describe the payment interaction before choosing a database or an HTTP framework. The client supplies an order identifier, a payment method reference, and a stable idempotency key. A successful authorization response reports the provider’s decision and Baodium’s operation identifier. A timeout leaves the outcome unresolved, so the client retrieves that operation rather than inventing a new payment.

POST /v1/orders/4471/payment-authorizations
Idempotency-Key: checkout-4471-attempt-1

{"payment_method_id":"pm_21"}

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
{"operation_id":"payop_783","status":"PENDING"}

The 202 Accepted response means Baodium accepted responsibility for the operation, and nothing more. The provider may not have authorized the payment yet. The client can call GET /v1/payment-operations/payop_783 to obtain a later result. The public contract must document whether the operation can expire, what the client should do while it is pending, and which response codes represent a business decline or an invalid request.

A useful database model separates the order, the intended payment operation, and individual provider attempts. Each serves a different purpose. An order records what the customer purchased. The operation records one intended authorization, its parameters, and its current state. An attempt records a specific interaction with the provider, including an unresolved result that may need reconciliation. This separation also appears in cloud provisioning, travel bookings, and jobs submitted through an API.

CREATE TABLE payment_operations (
  operation_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  idempotency_key text NOT NULL,
  request_hash text NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (order_id, idempotency_key)
);
CREATE INDEX payment_operations_by_order
  ON payment_operations (order_id, created_at DESC);

The unique constraint makes repeated submissions find the same operation. The request hash lets the service reject reuse of a key with different business parameters. The foreign key protects the relationship to the order. The lookup index supports order-history and reconciliation queries. The database can reject conflicting operation identities, but the provider retry contract and guarded state transitions still determine whether a second attempt produces another authorization.1

Operation, Record, and Message Identity

Checkout uses three kinds of identity, listed in Table Table. They are easy to mix up, and mixing them up is a common source of duplicate effects, so be precise about what each one names.

Identities used in the checkout workflow.
Identity What it identifies Example use
Record ID A stored business entity. Retrieve an order and its payment history.
Operation ID One intended business action. Recognize repeated attempts to authorize the same payment.
Message ID One published event. Recognize repeated delivery before applying a local update.

An order ID identifies the purchase. A single purchase can involve several payment operations, such as an authorization, a capture, and a refund, and each of them needs its own identity so that the application can tell a repeated attempt from a new action. When checkout retries an authorization after a lost response, it reuses the original operation ID. When it refunds part of the payment, it creates a new operation ID linked to that payment. A second partial refund gets its own ID as well, even if the amount is the same as the first, because it is a separate business action. The test is always the same. Is this the same intended action again, or a new one?

The idempotency key is how the operation ID reaches the provider, the cheque number in our earlier analogy. You send the key with the request, and the provider uses it to recognize repeated submissions of the same operation and return the original result instead of performing the operation again. Stripe, for example, accepts it in an Idempotency-Key HTTP header, and the pattern is common enough that the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) has drafted a standard for that header. Baodium stores its operation ID together with the key it sends, so every attempt and every recovery uses the same identity. The provider’s API contract then decides the details, such as how long the provider recognizes the key, which request fields must match, and whether a retry sent from another region receives the original result.

Message identity becomes necessary when a service publishes events through a broker. The producer assigns an ID when it creates the event and reuses that ID on every publication attempt, so a consumer can recognize an event it has already processed. You will use this later in the chapter, in the section on the transactional outbox.

Storing these relationships durably also helps the people who investigate problems. An engineer can start from an order, find its payment operations, and retrieve the provider references, without relying on request logs that may have been deleted by the time anyone looks.

Caller Identity and Permission

The operation identifier names the payment checkout is attempting. It says nothing about who is making the request. Imagine a merchant employee who can review orders but cannot refund them. Copying an earlier refund’s idempotency key does not give that employee permission to initiate another refund, even if the key matches a valid operation in the database.

We need to distinguish four things. The authenticated principal is the person or service making the request. The resource identity selects the order or payment. The operation identity allows safe retries of one intended action. The authority for the result is the service that may commit the business-state transition. In Baodium, Payment Service records whether a refund was accepted or completed. A successful identity check at the gateway cannot make that decision for it.

These checks run in a fixed order. After authentication, checkout verifies that the principal may access the order before returning a recorded operation or its status. Otherwise, someone who learns an operation ID could retrieve a payment result belonging to another merchant. When a request creates a new operation, the service also checks permission to perform that action. A permitted read of an order is not permission to modify its payment.

This distinction applies to a deployment controller as well. Its operation ID identifies a deployment attempt, while the caller’s permissions, the approved artifact, and the current deployment policy determine whether that attempt may proceed. Chapter 4 develops the checks across service boundaries, and Chapter 11 examines where those checks belong when several services share a workflow.

Recording Intent Before the Remote Call

Baodium’s revised checkout stores the authorization intent before it calls the provider. The record describes the action to perform and gives the outcome a place to go. If the process crashes after sending the request, another handler can read the record and see that an attempt was made, which identity it used, and what evidence is still needed before anything is retried.

The amount_minor value of 10000 represents $100.00 in USD. The server derives that amount and its currency from the order, and the payment-method reference is a provider token rather than a card number. The record is created before the external call, so provider_authorization_id is initially null. Its local operation ID and provider idempotency key are already durable.

If the handler crashes after the database commit, recovery can submit the recorded payment details under the original identity. It must not reconstruct an authorization from an order the customer may since have edited.

Repeated Requests and Conflicting Details

Suppose a caller requests a $100 authorization and then repeats the request with the same key but an amount of $1,000. If checkout returned the first result, it would hide the conflict, and if it submitted the new amount, it could create a payment the customer had never authorized. So checkout rejects the conflicting request before it contacts the provider.

To detect a conflict, checkout compares the fields that define the operation, which are the order, amount, currency, payment-method reference, operation type, and provider account. You can compare these fields directly, or compare a fingerprint, a hash calculated from the normalized values. Leave out fields that legitimately change between retries, such as attempt numbers and tracing headers. If you use fingerprints, give the normalization rules a version number, so that a later deployment can still interpret operations created by earlier code.

A matching request can retrieve the recorded outcome or the pending status, as long as the caller is allowed to see the order. Knowing an idempotency key should never give a caller extra access.

An idempotency key identifies a submission, but a customer can generate another key by clicking Pay again. Checkout also needs an order-level rule. While an authorization is pending or requires reconciliation, a second submission cannot create an independent authorization for that order.

Concurrent Duplicate Submissions

Two submissions can reach checkout at the same moment, and both can read an unpaid order. If each handler checks the order and then inserts a payment operation as a separate step, both can create an authorization. A test that sends the two requests one after the other will pass, because the second handler finds the operation the first one committed. Under concurrent load, both handlers can pass the check before either one inserts a record.

Baodium makes this decision inside a local database transaction. The handler locks the order row, checks the order’s current payment operation, and either returns that operation or creates a new one if the order’s payment state allows it. Every code path that can start a payment goes through this procedure, and the new operation and the order’s reference to it commit together. A concurrent submission then finds the existing operation, even if the browser sent a new key, and a request with conflicting payment details is rejected by the comparison described earlier.

You can also have the database enforce the rule, so that a code path that skips this procedure still cannot create a second authorization. In PostgreSQL, a partial unique index can allow at most one active authorization per order.

With this index in place, a second insert for the same order fails while an earlier authorization is unresolved or successful, no matter which code path tries it. A declined or voided authorization falls outside the index, so the customer can still try another payment method. A unique constraint on the provider idempotency key gives the same protection for keys.

The transaction ends before the provider call, and its database connection goes back to the pool. You saw why in Chapters 1 and 2. If the transaction were still open during the provider call, every slow provider response would occupy a database connection and a row lock, and a provider slowdown would soon become a connection-pool outage. Checkout sends the stored identity and payment details only after the transaction has committed.

Two handlers can still submit the same operation, for example when a retry overlaps the original call, but both use the same provider key. The order-level check prevents independent authorizations for an unresolved payment, and the provider’s idempotency handles repeated submissions of the operation checkout chose.

Atomic Updates and Transaction Isolation

The duplicate-payment problem was one example of concurrent requests reading the same state. Inventory presents another. Suppose two customers try to reserve the last unit of a product. A handler that reads the available quantity and later writes the reduced value can approve both reservations if the two reads overlap. The application may have checked that stock was available, but the check and the change were two different database operations.

For a quantity stored in one PostgreSQL row, we can make the condition part of the update itself.

UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - 1
WHERE sku = 'sku-9' AND available > 0
RETURNING available;

If the statement returns no row, the reservation failed. PostgreSQL rechecks the condition after a concurrent update has committed, so two transactions cannot both reduce the same last unit below zero through this statement. The reservation record and the quantity update still belong in the same local transaction. A failure to insert the reservation must roll back the quantity change.

This is a form of conditional update. It is useful when the invariant can be enforced on the row being changed. Constraints that span several rows need more care. At PostgreSQL’s default READ COMMITTED isolation level, two transactions can each read an apparently valid set of rows and then make different updates that, together, violate a rule. Locking the relevant records or using SERIALIZABLE transactions with a retry policy may be necessary. The retry must repeat the database transaction, without repeating an external payment or notification.2

The distinction matters when designing reservations, account transfers, booking limits, and approval quotas. An idempotency key can recognize a repeated request, while a transaction constraint establishes whether that request may change the current state.

Provider Idempotency Guarantees

That last step relies on what the provider guarantees, because a local record cannot stop an external service from performing the same write twice. Before relying on idempotency keys, the payments engineers checked four things in the provider’s documentation, then confirmed each one in the provider’s test environment. They checked the scope of a key, what happens when two requests with the same key arrive together, which recovery methods the provider offers, and how long the provider retains a key.

Scope matters because a key may be valid only for a particular account or operation type, so recovery has to use the same account and endpoint as the original request. Concurrent handling matters because some providers respond with an in-progress or conflict status when two matching requests overlap, and checkout must treat that response as a signal to wait and check again, not as a failure that justifies a new authorization. Recovery methods differ between providers. One may let you look up a payment by key, another may give you a durable payment object to retrieve, and a third may only let you resend the request with the original key. Retention differs too, and some providers recognize a key for as little as a day.

These details belong in the integration contract, because they decide which recovery actions are available to you. If a provider gives you no way to deduplicate or look up an interrupted write, you need another recovery channel, which may mean an operator contacting the provider directly.

Persisting Provider Outcomes

A confirmed authorization lets checkout record success, and a definitive decline lets it record failure. The difficult cases are interruptions that happen before checkout can save either result. Table Table lists the points where that can happen.

Recovery information available after an interruption.
Interruption Recovery information
Before the local intent commits No provider call is permitted. A repeated request can create or retrieve the intent.
After intent commit, before submission A pending operation exists. Recovery uses its stored identity.
After provider authorization, before local result commit The local operation is unresolved. Recovery obtains provider evidence.
After local result commit, before the browser receives it A repeated request retrieves the recorded result.

From checkout’s side, the second and third rows produce the same evidence, a request with no reply. In both cases, a recovery worker finds a pending operation with no provider reference. You might think a submitted flag would tell them apart, but it cannot. The process could stop after setting the flag and before sending the request, or after sending the request and before setting the flag, so the flag does not reliably tell you whether the provider received anything. This is the Two Generals’ Problem from the start of the chapter, showing up in a single table column.

The worker has to use the original operation identity to get evidence from the provider. The recovery process looks at two groups of operations, those already marked for reconciliation and pending operations that have been waiting longer than their expected processing time. The second group catches processes that crashed without ever reaching an exception handler.

Once the result is confirmed, the operation update and the matching order transition commit together in one local transaction. The record includes the provider reference, when there is one, and the evidence used to establish the outcome, so later requests can retrieve the result and anyone investigating can see how it was decided.

State Transitions and Delayed Results

The payment operation describes one action. The order describes the progress of the whole checkout, which also depends on inventory, fulfillment, and cancellation, so an authorization can succeed while checkout is still waiting for another step. Figure Figure shows the payment-related order states and the transitions between them, and Table Table describes each state.

Payment-related order states. Each operation also records its own identity, outcome, and provider evidence.
Order state Meaning for checkout
PENDING_PAYMENT Payment has not been confirmed. Any submitted authorization has an attached operation record.
RECONCILIATION_PENDING The authorization requires recovery. An independent replacement authorization is blocked.
PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED Authorization is confirmed. Checkout can continue according to its inventory policy.
PAYMENT_FAILED The current authorization has a definitive unsuccessful outcome.
MANUAL_REVIEW Recovery requires an operator. An unresolved payment still blocks an independent replacement.

When a payment fails definitively, for example because the card is declined, the customer may choose another payment method. The new authorization gets a new operation ID, the earlier operation is retained in the payment history, and the order records which operation is current.

Now picture a recovery worker that reads the order, contacts the provider, and receives a response after another handler has already updated the order. If the worker applies its result using only the order ID, it can overwrite newer progress. Checking the state name is not enough either, because an order can return to a payment-pending state for a later operation. Baodium checks the current operation ID, the expected state, and the record version before updating the order.

Every update to an order increments its version. If another handler has changed the record since the worker read it, the expected version no longer matches and the statement updates zero rows. This approach is known as optimistic concurrency control, and you will meet it in almost every system that lets several processes update the same record. The statement runs inside the same transaction that records the operation’s confirmed result, and if it updates zero rows, the handler rolls back and reloads the records before deciding what to do. Another worker may already have recorded the same result, the order may have advanced for a valid reason, or the provider’s evidence may conflict with an earlier result. Unexpected evidence is stored for investigation rather than discarded.

Cancellations show why checkout compares the current order state with the provider’s result before applying it. If the customer cancels while the authorization is in progress and the authorization then succeeds, the order must not continue through normal checkout just because the payment went through. The handler records the provider’s result through a recovery path for canceled orders, and that path will usually need to void the authorization.

Decision review

The status lookup says NOT_FOUND

A payment authorization timed out four minutes ago, and the operation record is in RECONCILIATION_PENDING . A recovery worker calls the provider’s status endpoint with the operation identifier and receives NOT_FOUND. The customer is waiting, and support has asked whether the customer can retry the purchase.

Treat NOT_FOUND as proof that no authorization exists, mark the operation failed, and let the customer try again.

Submit the original request again under the same idempotency key.

Leave the operation unresolved and retry the lookup after a delay, escalating to manual review at the recovery deadline.

A is safe only if the provider guarantees that NOT_FOUND rules out both a completed authorization and an original request that could still complete. Without that guarantee, the original request might complete after the lookup, and a new purchase would then reserve the customer’s money twice.

B depends on the provider’s idempotency contract. The provider must still recognize the original key, the request must match the original operation, and a repeat must not create a second authorization. If those conditions are met, the provider either completes the original operation or returns its recorded result. Section Section lists the contract details to check, including how long the provider remembers a key.

C leaves the operation unresolved without sending another authorization, which is the safe choice while the provider’s guarantees are unknown. If repeated lookups cannot establish the outcome, the recovery deadline passes the case to an operator. The cost is a longer pending purchase, so the customer and support staff need a way to see its status.

Provider Reconciliation

Reconciliation resolves a local operation using evidence from the provider. That evidence can come from a status lookup, from an authenticated notification the provider sends, or from a repeated request covered by the provider’s idempotency contract. Whatever the source, a recovery worker should act only on what it can prove. Three details need particular care. They are what a missing result means, how long a request can safely be repeated, and which worker is responsible for each piece of recovery work.

Unresolved Provider Outcomes

As the decision above showed, a NOT_FOUND response can look like a final verdict, but the original request may still be in progress and can commit a moment after the lookup. Read “not found” as a statement about the lookup at that moment, not about the payment. It tells you only that the provider had no completed record when it responded. Before you treat absence as a definitive failure, you need an authoritative lookup and an assurance from the provider that the earlier attempt can no longer complete. A searchable payment history covering several days gives you neither of those on its own.

If the provider lets you resubmit with the same key and identical parameters, recovery can use that instead. Otherwise, the operation needs further reconciliation or a review by an operator.

Retention and Recovery Deadlines

Your local operation records need to cover the whole period during which delayed jobs, callbacks, recovery workers, or operators might repeat an action. The provider’s retention needs a separate check, because the two periods are often different.

Suppose Baodium retains operation records for fourteen days, but the provider recognizes duplicate keys for only seven. On day eight, a worker can still read the original key from Baodium’s database, yet submitting it may create a new authorization, because the provider has forgotten the key. Recovery after that point needs durable evidence from the provider or an operator procedure, and before a worker sends an old queued request, it should check whether the provider still recognizes duplicates for that operation. These periods are only examples. Your integration needs the provider’s actual guarantees, including any difference between how long it recognizes idempotency keys and how long it retains payment records. A payment may still be retrievable long after its request key has expired.

You also need a policy for deleting local records. If an old request arrives after its deduplication record has been deleted, the application might treat it as new. Depending on the workflow, you can retain a smaller record of the final outcome after deleting the details, or reject expired operations by issuing operation identities from the server with an enforced validity period.

Finally, define an escalation deadline, after which an operator becomes responsible for an unresolved case. Reaching the deadline tells you nothing new about whether the authorization succeeded. It only decides who handles the case from then on.

Lease-Based Recovery Workers

Recovery work usually runs in background workers, and two workers should not process the same operation at the same time. A common approach is for a worker to claim an operation for a limited period before processing it, much as you might book a meeting room for an hour so that another group does not use it at the same time. This time-limited claim is called a lease. It reduces overlapping work, and because it expires, another worker can take over if the first one crashes.

Baodium stores an owner token and an expiry time with each claim. A worker can claim pending operations with a statement like the one below, which uses PostgreSQL’s SKIP LOCKED option so that concurrent workers pick different rows instead of waiting for one another.

The expiry is calculated with the database’s clock rather than the worker’s, so differences between machine clocks cannot give the same lease to two workers for overlapping periods. Renewals and result updates check both the token and the expiry, so a worker whose lease has expired can no longer update the record.

Why is the token needed when the expiry already limits the claim? Let’s consider a worker that pauses for a long time, during a long garbage-collection pause, say, or after its virtual machine is suspended. When it resumes, its lease may have expired and another worker may have claimed the operation. Without the token check, the first worker could overwrite the second worker’s result. With it, the first worker’s update matches zero rows. A token used this way is often called a fencing token, and we will examine the same idea again when this book discusses database failover and shard ownership.

The paused worker might still receive a late response from the provider. Expiring a local lease does not cancel a request already running at the provider, so the replacement worker must use the same operation identity and the provider’s recovery protocol.

Batch size also affects correctness. A worker that claims many records and processes them one at a time may not reach the last ones before their leases expire, and another worker will then process them as well. Claiming small batches as capacity becomes available, as the statement above does, reduces this overlap.

Synchronous responses, recovery workers, and provider notifications all record results through the same guarded procedure. Notifications are authenticated, for example by verifying the provider’s signature, and matched to the stored operation, account, and payment details before they can change the order.

Compensation After Partial Completion

The recovery steps above dealt with retries and uncertain outcomes. Another problem appears when one part of an operation commits and a later part fails. A travel booking provides an example. The site reserves a flight, then a hotel, then a rental car. If the car company has nothing available, the site cannot roll back the airline’s database. It has to send the airline a cancellation, which is a new action in its own right. Checkout faces the same situation when payment succeeds but the items turn out to be out of stock, or the customer cancels before fulfillment begins. The payment has already happened in another system, so a database rollback cannot undo it. Checkout has to perform a second business action that counteracts the first, which is called compensation.

Compensation adds a new action rather than deleting the old one. After a captured payment, a refund creates a new credit linked to the original charge, and the customer’s statement shows both. Depending on the provider’s contract, the original processing fee may not come back. Canceling a shipment may need a request to the carrier, and an email that has already been delivered cannot be recalled at all. When you design recovery, you need to know what each corrective action can achieve.

This is also why the business owner, not only the engineering team, needs to approve each compensating action before it becomes an automated recovery rule. Releasing a reservation and refunding a payment may both be technically possible, but releasing stock after a merchant has already packed the order could go against the agreed fulfillment policy. Engineers can list the states the system can reach, but deciding what the company should do in each of them is a business decision. Table Table shows the counteractions available for each confirmed effect in checkout.

Compensation depends on the current business state and the receiving service’s contract.
Confirmed effect Possible counteraction
Uncaptured authorization Void or cancel the authorization.
Captured payment Refund the permitted amount.
Inventory reservation Release that reservation.
Fulfillment request Cancel if fulfillment has not passed the cancellation point.

Suppose an authorization succeeds and the inventory service then definitively rejects the reservation. Checkout needs to void the uncaptured authorization. The void is a new operation, so it gets its own operation ID and provider key, and its stored details identify the authorization being voided.

Baodium creates the compensation operation and changes the order to COMPENSATION_PENDING in one local transaction, and a worker then processes that operation. If the process stops after the transaction commits, another worker finds the pending void and continues. A confirmed void completes the payment side of the compensation, while a lost response means the void itself needs reconciliation, just like the original authorization. If the provider definitively refuses the void, the case enters COMPENSATION_FAILED and an operator is assigned. If the payment had already been captured, the next action might be a refund instead.

The inventory side can be uncertain too. A rejected reservation request is clear, because Inventory said no. A request that timed out is not, because Inventory may have reserved the stock and the reply was lost on the way back. Before checkout can mark the order as fully compensated, it has to resolve that operation and release any reservation it created, so a single order can have several recovery actions outstanding.

A sequence of local transactions across different systems, in which each step has a compensating action, is called a saga. The term comes from research on long-running database transactions.3 It also describes the coordination of bookings, provisioning, and other multi-service operations. The saga’s durable record tracks which steps completed, which operations are unresolved, and which counteractions are still required. Compensation depends on the business dependencies and on which actions are still possible. Once a parcel has been dispatched, for example, cancellation is no longer available, and recovery becomes a returns process.

If your team uses a workflow engine such as Temporal or Step Functions from Amazon Web Services (AWS), you might expect it to handle all of this for you. These engines record which steps have completed, retry failed steps, and run compensation logic, so you write far less bookkeeping yourself. You still need everything this chapter describes, though. A workflow engine retries a step whose response was lost, just as your own code would, so each step that calls another system still needs a stable operation identity and an idempotent request. And the engine cannot decide which compensating action your business considers correct.

When we review a multi-step operation, we can walk through each point at which processing might stop and ask three questions. Which completed actions would need compensation? Which outcomes would need investigation? Where would that work be recorded? Those three lists define the recovery paths the application has to support.

Events and the Transactional Outbox

A closely related problem appears whenever a service updates its database and also publishes an event for other services. Suppose Order Service commits an order transition and then crashes before publishing the corresponding event. Downstream consumers never receive the change. If Order Service publishes first instead, the broker might accept the event and the database transaction might then fail, so consumers receive an event for a change that never happened. Either order fails for the same reason. You cannot update two separate systems in one atomic step. This is sometimes called the dual-write problem, and it is one of the most common sources of quiet data inconsistency in microservice systems.

The transactional outbox avoids it by storing the unpublished event in the service’s own database until a separate relay publishes it (Figure Figure). The name comes from the tray on an office desk. A clerk finishes a letter and drops it in the outbox as part of the same task, and the mail room collects it later. The clerk does not stop to deliver it personally, and the letter is not lost if the clerk goes home. In the same way, Order Service writes the state change and an event record in one database transaction, and the relay later reads the committed records and sends them to the broker.

Here, advance validates the transition, checks the expected version, and increments it. If the transition is rejected, the transaction aborts, so no event can claim that the transition happened.

The relay marks an event as published only after the broker acknowledges it. If the relay stops between the broker’s acknowledgment and that local update, it publishes the event again after it restarts, with the same message ID. The relay can find new records by polling the outbox table, or by reading the database’s change log with a change-data-capture tool such as Debezium. Either way, consumers must handle duplicates.

A consumer can handle repeated delivery by recording the message ID in the same database transaction as its business update.

Both repositories use the same transactional database, and the marker insert relies on a uniqueness constraint, so if two copies of the same message arrive together, only one insert succeeds. If the transaction fails, the marker and the reservation update roll back together and the message is not acknowledged, so the broker delivers it again. If the commit succeeds but the acknowledgment is lost, the next delivery finds the marker and skips the update. This consumer is idempotent in the same sense as the light switch labeled “on.”

The markers need to outlive the period during which the broker might redeliver or replay a message. The reservation also needs its own business identity, because two distinct messages could request the same reservation, and their different message IDs would both pass the delivery check.

If you use Kafka, you may have read that it supports exactly-once processing. That guarantee is genuine, but it covers reading from Kafka topics and writing to Kafka topics inside Kafka transactions. It does not extend to updates in your own database or to calls to an external provider, so a consumer that writes to a database still needs a check like the one above. Chapter 12 returns to event delivery in much more depth, including ordering and replay.

Recovery Metrics and Failure Testing

Recovery code runs rarely, and on most days it has nothing to do. A broken recovery worker produces the same metrics as a healthy one with an empty queue, until a customer contacts support about a payment that was never resolved. Recovery needs monitoring that shows whether it is making progress, and tests that exercise it on purpose.

Durable operation records make both possible, because they let you measure unfinished work directly. Baodium tracks the number of unresolved operations and the age of the oldest one, and it alerts when that age exceeds the expected recovery time. Age is usually the better alert. The graph of unresolved operations can be a flat line while a single operation goes unresolved for days, but the age of the oldest one rises every minute until someone deals with it. After a provider outage, the engineers compare the rate of new unresolved operations with the rate of recovery completions to see whether the backlog is shrinking, the same reasoning you used for queues in Chapter 2.

Compensation has its own monitoring and escalation path, because an order can be marked canceled while its payment void is still pending. The customer’s order page and the support view show these outcomes separately, so neither suggests the payment has been resolved when it has not.

The engineers also compare local and provider records in both directions. Starting from local operations finds missing or conflicting provider results. Starting from provider records finds authorizations with no matching local operation, including any created by older or faulty code. If you check only the provider IDs already stored locally, you will miss the authorizations whose responses were lost, and those are the ones that caused the original incident. Many providers offer daily settlement or transaction reports that make this second comparison practical. Accountants have done this for centuries under the name reconciliation, which is where the term comes from.

Operators use controlled recovery actions that obey the same rules as the application. A manual retry reuses the stored operation and respects the provider’s retention limits. A replacement authorization needs an established outcome for the previous operation and a recorded business reason.

Before release, the engineers interrupted processing on purpose at three points, after the intent committed, after the provider accepted the request, and after the local result committed. They also tested concurrent submissions, late responses, expired leases, and repeated event delivery. For each test, they inspected both the local records and the effects at the provider, using the provider’s test environment. When a test lost the authorization response, recovery had to resolve the original operation without creating another authorization. A successful HTTP response at the end of the test could not prove that, because a duplicate authorization would be visible only at the provider.

Versioned Change Authorization

Identity rules like these are just as useful well beyond payments. Let’s consider a deployment pipeline in which Jenkins submits a production change to a validation service before deploying it. The service evaluates the request and records its decision, but the HTTP response never reaches Jenkins. While Jenkins retries, an administrator publishes a new policy revision. Now the validation service has two jobs. It must recognize the retry and return the decision it already made, and it must still make sure that Jenkins has a valid authorization at the moment the deployment starts.

The API needs three distinct identifiers to separate those jobs. The change ID identifies the proposed deployment and its immutable target, such as an artifact digest and destination environment. The request key identifies a retryable submission under that change and its parameters. The evaluation ID identifies the decision produced under a particular policy revision. Reusing the request key with different parameters is a conflict. Repeating it with the same parameters can retrieve the recorded evaluation. A new policy revision may justify a new evaluation, while the original operation history is retained for audit.

The database needs versioned policy records, change records, and evaluation records. Its evaluation record contains the change ID, policy revision, input digest, decision, evaluation time, and reason codes. The API returns ALLOW, DENY, or INDETERMINATE. When Jira, which stores the change approvals, is unavailable, the validator lacks approval evidence. It records INDETERMINATE, refuses to authorize deployment, and schedules a retry or review, which is the validator’s equivalent of an unresolved payment.

CREATE TABLE policy_revision (
  revision bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  body_sha256 text NOT NULL,
  published_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE change_evaluation (
  evaluation_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  change_id uuid NOT NULL,
  request_key text NOT NULL,
  input_sha256 text NOT NULL,
  policy_revision bigint NOT NULL
    REFERENCES policy_revision(revision),
  decision text NOT NULL CHECK (
    decision IN ('ALLOW', 'DENY', 'INDETERMINATE')),
  evaluated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE(change_id, request_key)
);

The unique constraint makes one submission identity authoritative within a change. Application code must compare the stored input digest when a conflict occurs and return the earlier result only for an identical request. A production system would also bind the deployment target and approver evidence to the change record. Before execution, the enforcement endpoint must establish whether the earlier evaluation is still eligible under the currently active policy. That later check is separate from making the initial submission idempotent. Appendix B develops the full design and its failure cases.

You will meet this distinction in bookings whose price changes after a quote, infrastructure provisioning after an account policy update, and bank transfers that need a fresh risk decision before execution. The operation identifier retrieves earlier attempts and results, while the decision to execute still depends on the current policy.

Summary

Here is the idea from this chapter that you will use most often. A timeout tells you only that you stopped waiting. Once you accept that, the design changes in a predictable way. Before calling a system you do not control, you write down what you intend to do and give that intent a name, so that every retry, every recovery worker, and every operator can refer to the same action.

The rest of the design is built on that record. The order-level rule stops a second click from starting a second payment. Guarded updates stop a late response from overwriting newer progress. Reconciliation settles the unknown cases from evidence instead of hope, and compensation handles the cases where one step succeeded and a later one did not. When you review a design, try walking through each point where the process could stop, and ask what record would let someone else finish the job. If there is no such record, you have found the next incident.

Payments make the uncertainty easy to see, but the same reasoning applies to a booking, a provisioning request, or a deployment approval. While those operations wait, though, they still occupy workers and connections on the calling side, and Chapter 4 looks at what happens to a service when the dependency it waits on slows down.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Repeated attempts for one authorization can be recognized through the provider’s documented idempotency and recovery mechanisms, within their scope and retention limits.
Condition that tests it & A response is lost, or a delayed result arrives after another checkout update.
Constraint or invariant & Baodium and the payment provider commit separately. A local rollback cannot remove a provider authorization.
Evidence and uncertainty & The opening incident produced two authorizations after one lost response. Recovery tests inspect provider effects as well as local records.

Still unknown: the outcome of an interrupted provider call, including requests still in progress and requests no longer covered by duplicate recognition.
Signal and evaluation window & Track the age of the oldest unresolved operation, and compare local state with provider evidence during recovery.
Control and decision & Recover the existing operation while its outcome is unresolved. Permit a replacement authorization only after establishing the earlier outcome and confirming that the business workflow allows another payment.
Owner and review trigger & The payment-service owner defines operation identity and recovery. Operations staff manage escalated cases through an audited procedure. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.
